criteria.descriptor: Correctly characterizes both options: hosted = per-token/usage pricing, provider-managed infra behind an SLA, rate limits/network latency, generally stronger frontier quality, data sent to a third party (with no-train/retention controls available); self-hosted open-weight = fixed GPU cost, self-managed serving stack (vLLM/TGI/Ollama), data stays in-house, full control to fine-tune/quantize, quality bounded by the chosen model size. Full marks require no false claims such as 'self-hosting is always cheaper', 'hosted always trains on your data', or 'open-weight models are free'.

Addresses all four required dimensions (cost structure, data privacy/control, operational burden, capability/quality) AND delivers an explicit recommendation. Deduct for each omitted dimension or for stopping at a comparison with no recommendation.

Ties the recommendation to the prototype/early-stage context rather than asserting it: reasons about volume-based cost break-even, weighs time-to-ship and quality-validation against operational burden, and names a concrete trigger (e.g., higher/steady volume, cost, or data-residency requirements) for later switching to self-hosting.

Organized (per-dimension) and easy to follow, uses precise vocabulary (per-token vs fixed cost, serving stack, data residency, rate limits, open-weight), and states an unambiguous, actionable recommendation.

expected_answer_points: Cost structure contrast: hosted is usage-based per-token with no fixed infra (cheaper at low/bursty volume); self-hosting is a largely fixed GPU cost that only pays off at high, steady throughput — there is a volume break-even point

Data privacy/control: self-hosting keeps ticket data in-house (helps with sensitive/regulated data and data residency), whereas hosted sends data to a third party — but notes that no-training/zero-retention/enterprise terms mean hosted does not automatically train on or expose your data

Operational burden: self-hosting requires owning GPU provisioning, a serving stack (e.g., vLLM/TGI/Ollama), scaling, uptime, monitoring and upgrades; a hosted API offloads this behind an SLA (trading it for rate limits and network latency)

Capability/quality: frontier hosted models generally outperform a small open-weight model on hard reasoning, but a narrow task like summarization may not need that; open-weight adds control to fine-tune/quantize and avoid forced version deprecation
Gives a clear recommendation: use a hosted API for the prototype stage

Justifies the recommendation with the early-stage context: fastest to ship, no infra, low cost at low volume, and strong quality to validate the feature — with an explicit trigger (rising volume/cost or data-residency needs) for revisiting self-hosting later
common_pitfalls: Claims self-hosting is 'always cheaper' because there is no per-token bill, ignoring that a fixed GPU cost dominates at low or bursty prototype volume where hosted per-token usage is far cheaper
Assumes any hosted API necessarily trains on or leaks customer data, ignoring no-training/zero-retention and enterprise terms — or the reverse, dismissing privacy entirely
Recommends self-hosting for a prototype while underestimating the operational burden (GPU provisioning, serving stack, scaling, uptime, monitoring, upgrades)
Conflates 'open-weight' with fully 'open-source' or assumes open-weight models are free, overlooking that you still pay for compute and that the license/training data may be restricted
Assumes a small 8B open-weight model matches frontier hosted quality, or conversely insists you always need a frontier model even for a narrow summarization task
Produces a comparison but no clear recommendation, or gives a recommendation not tied to the early-stage context (a vague 'it depends' with no break-even or triggering conditions)
reference_answer:
Cost structure: A hosted API is usage-based, billed per input/output token, with zero fixed infrastructure. A self-hosted open-weight model is mostly a fixed cost — you pay for the GPU whether it is busy or idle. So hosted is cheaper at low or bursty volume, while self-hosting only wins once you have high, steady throughput that amortizes the GPU. The right question is where the break-even volume sits, not which is 'cheaper' in the abstract.

Data privacy/control: Self-hosting keeps ticket text inside your own environment, which helps with sensitive or regulated data and data-residency requirements. With a hosted API the data leaves to a third party — though reputable providers offer no-training / zero-retention and enterprise terms, so 'hosted = they train on your data' is not automatically true.

Operational burden: Self-hosting means you own GPU provisioning, the serving stack (vLLM/TGI/Ollama), autoscaling, uptime, monitoring, and model upgrades. A hosted API offloads all of that behind an SLA; your cost is network latency and rate limits.

Capability/quality: Frontier hosted models generally beat a small 8B open-weight model on hard reasoning, but ticket summarization is narrow, so a small model may be good enough. Open-weight gives control — you can fine-tune, quantize, and avoid version deprecation — at the price of doing that work yourself.

Recommendation: For a prototype, start with a hosted API. It ships fastest with no infra, is cheap at low volume, and gives strong quality to validate whether the feature is even worth it. Instrument real token volume, cost, latency, and privacy needs; revisit self-hosting only if volume/cost or data-residency requirements later justify it.
